items.stem: Why can comparing two String objects with == give a surprising result in Java?

options.text: == compares object references, so two Strings with equal content may still be different objects
options.rationale: Correct: == checks reference identity for objects; equals() compares content.
== compares references for objects, not content.

options.text: Strings cannot be compared at all
options.rationale: Strings can be compared with equals() (and compareTo()).

options.text: == converts both Strings to numbers first
options.rationale: No numeric conversion happens when comparing Strings.

items.explanation: Correct: == checks reference identity for objects; equals() compares content.

items.stem: Select TWO statements that correctly distinguish method overriding from overloading in Java.

options.text: Overriding redefines an inherited method with the same signature in a subclass
options.rationale: Correct: overriding keeps the signature and changes behavior in a subclass.

options.text: Overloading declares multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists
options.rationale: Correct: overloading varies the parameter list within the same scope.

options.text: Overriding must change the method name
options.rationale: Overriding keeps the same name and signature.

options.text: Overloading and overriding are the same thing

items.explanation: Correct: overriding keeps the signature and changes behavior in a subclass.

items.stem: You need a collection that stores unique elements with no duplicates. Which Java collection type fits best?

options.rationale: Correct: a Set stores unique elements and rejects duplicates.
A List allows duplicates and preserves insertion order.
A Map stores key-value pairs, not a plain set of unique values.

options.text: Array of fixed size with manual checks
options.rationale: A raw array does not enforce uniqueness without extra manual code; Set does it directly.

items.explanation: Correct: a Set stores unique elements and rejects duplicates.
